stories.headline: What WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert's retirement means
stories.summary: What does the league need from its next commissioner after Cathy Engelbert retires? Is the WNBA better off now than when she took over?
stories.byline: Michael Voepel and Kendra Andrews and Kareem Copeland
stories.body:
The WNBA has changed substantially since Cathy Engelbert -- who announced Friday she will retire at the end of this year -- took over in 2019. Her tenure included two collective bargaining agreements, an enormous increase in franchise valuations, expansion that will reach 18 teams by 2030 and a much greater global footprint.

Engelbert gets a lot of credit for that, but she also received plenty of criticism in her seven years, especially regarding her relationships with players.

What legacy does Engelbert leave behind? What traits should the WNBA be looking for in its next commissioner? And what will that leader's priorities be in their first year? ESPN examines the WNBA commissioner's job: the person who is leaving it and what awaits the person who takes over.

What is Engelbert's legacy as WNBA commissioner?

Michael Voepel: I've covered the WNBA since Day 1 and have worked with every WNBA leader. (They were called presidents until the title was changed for Engelbert's tenure.) Each brought her own skill set and led the league at different stages of growth. Val Ackerman was a lawyer who was instrumental in launching the league. Donna Orender worked at boosting visibility while also keeping the league alive during the global financial crisis of 2007-09. Laurel J. Richie was the first Black woman to take the league's leadership role, and Lisa Borders, also a Black woman with an extensive business background, navigated the more public actions players began to take with social justice initiatives.

Engelbert, previously CEO at Deloitte, came from the financial world, and at her first news conference in 2019 she stated her goals as expanding the league, making it financially viable and improving the player experience. All of those things have happened. Whatever Engelbert's missteps, the league is in a far better place as she leaves it.

Kendra Andrews: Though Engelbert had many wins during her tenure, I think the past year marked with tension with her players will overshadow everything else. When Napheesa Collier sat at the podium during her exit interview in September 2025 and shared the most public criticism an athlete has voiced about a commissioner, and then had her peers back her up, that became Engelbert's legacy. Since then, there has hardly been any positive review of Engelbert from WNBA players.

People will remember the boos that rained down on her at the Commissioner's Cup finals and WNBA All-Star Weekends. They will remember how long and contentious the 2026 CBA negotiations were, and they will remember how multiple figures around the league called for a new leader.

Two things can be true: Engelbert drove a lot of success in the league, and she was not beloved by players. The latter is what she will be remembered for.

Kareem Copeland: Time will likely forget the dustups -- the rocky relationship with players, slow-playing advancements in travel and other leaguewide accommodations, a tendency to be overconcerned about the older ownership groups while the league was growing with owners willing to invest more heavily. The bottom line is the league will have expanded to its highest number of teams in league history when Detroit and Cleveland arrive, expanded to the most games in league history, signed the biggest media deal in women's sports history and landed a CBA that transformed the league into a new era with the first million-dollar salaries. When people look back in 10-20 years, that's what will be remembered.

What were Engelbert's biggest wins as WNBA commissioner?

Andrews: Executing the WNBA bubble during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 was a huge accomplishment for Engelbert. The 22-game season played in Florida against the backdrop of a deadly pandemic and national upheaval following the deaths of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor shined a new spotlight on the WNBA. It allowed the league to dedicate that season to social injustices, but also the viewership and level of play produced in the Wubble set the league up for a level of success over the next five years no one could have expected, especially given the circumstances. That condensed 2020 season, which occurred on the heels of the 2020 CBA agreement, set the W up for growth and exposure that has helped get the league to where it is today.

Copeland: The 2026 CBA is the easy answer, and navigating the environment around COVID and the racial injustices of 2020 were massive wins. But the simple act of moving to chartered flights, despite Engelbert's hesitation to do so for years, was so much more than a convenience move. That affected player health, how the league could schedule games, player safety and just the overall cadence of how teams operate throughout the season. Watching entire teams standing next to the traveling public at baggage claim was a sight to see. The one simple act touched on so many areas throughout the league that it's funny to think that it was just in 2022 that the New York Liberty were fined $500,000 for chartering flights.

Voepel: From a purely financial aspect, the fact that franchise valuations skyrocketed during Engelbert's tenure has been her biggest win. That's what led to improved travel, facilities and expansion. When James Dolan put the New York Liberty on the market in November 2017, he essentially said the team was of no value to him. Joe and Clara Wu Tsai bought the franchise in early 2019 for between $10-15 million. Now the Liberty have been valued as high as $600 million. The popularity of the individual players like Caitlin Clark and the league as a whole have greatly increased what the franchises are worth. But those increases happened with Engelbert at the helm.

In what areas did Engelbert struggle as commissioner?

Andrews: One piece of feedback from a player is that Engelbert was too reactionary. Rarely was she -- or the league -- ahead of the problems facing the WNBA and its players; player safety and online hate and abuse are examples. When it comes to the Internet, there is only so much that can be done. But the complaint was rooted in how much the issue escalated before the league publicly addressed it.

Some also found Engelbert's reaction to those issues to be lackluster. In September 2024, Engelbert failed to condemn racist and vitriolic behavior surrounding the Caitlin Clark-Angel Reese rivalry, instead telling CNBC that rivalries are good for the league. She later said she "missed the mark" with her initial statement and said it was a learning moment for her. She followed that by saying there is "no room for racism, misogyny [and] homophobia in the WNBA," but it was another missed opportunity to swiftly shut down a topic that has since grown into a major issue in WNBA discourse.

Voepel: To Kendra's points, Engelbert misjudged how to respond to players' concerns and wasn't able to build enough allies among either the owners or the players.

Some detractors also might point to the 2022 capital raise, when the WNBA sold a 16% equity stake to investors for $75 million, as a big mistake by Engelbert. But that move has to be taken in the context of when it happened: The WNBA badly needed that cash infusion, and the league's rapid growth since then was hardly expected. In early 2022, the "Caitlin Clark Effect" had yet to fully blossom -- it took off in 2023, her junior year at Iowa -- and the WNBA was still recovering from the 2020 pandemic season. So I don't see that capital raise as a failure so much as unfortunate timing, taking the circumstances into account.

Who might be in the discussions to take the job next?

Voepel: Bethany Donaphin, head of league operations, knows well what the commissioner's job entails and briefly played in the WNBA after her college career at Stanford.

Two other names some have suggested are former player Swin Cash and soon-to-retire Los Angeles Sparks forward Nneka Ogwumike, the longtime president of the players association. Cash has management experience from her time as a senior vice president with the NBA's New Orleans Pelicans. Ogwumike has plenty of experience with the league thanks to her involvement in two past CBAs, but she has been on the opposite side of the table. As commissioner, she would need to work for the owners.

Ultimately, this is a huge hire for Silver, who will be appointing the head of the WNBA for the third time since he became NBA commissioner in 2014.

What does the WNBA need from Engelbert's successor, especially in the first year?
Voepel: First off, repairing the relationship between both current and former players and the commissioner's office. That wasn't Engelbert's strength, and it damaged the perception of her tenure. The new commissioner must establish trust with the players. But the players must bear their share of responsibility in this, too. It has been easy for them to put the commissioner or the league on blast for everything they don't like or anything that went wrong in the past few years, even when that hasn't been constructive.

It would seem likely that any new commissioner will have a "honeymoon" period in which many players might be happy just to have someone different. But for the relationship to grow from that, both parties need to communicate and have respect for each other.

What skills or attributes does the next commissioner need?

Voepel: The WNBA commissioner needs to be an accomplished diplomat. There are so many constituencies involved in running a league: Obviously, there are the players. There are owners -- and remember, the commissioner works for them -- many of whom have been with the league for many years and others who are still learning the ropes. There are the fans -- some of whom have followed the league for decades; some who haven't. There are businesses and sponsors who have been with the WNBA a long time but still need to feel appreciated, and those that are new and must be cultivated. And there's the fact that the WNBA commissioner has a boss: the NBA commissioner.

The new commissioner will have to deal with an ever-growing media contingent and fanbase -- some of whom have followed the league for decades and some who haven't.

Engelbert's successor has to find a better way to navigate the racial tensions that everyone knows exist but are challenging to talk about in a constructive way. There are social issues that always seem to get magnified in women's sports.

The WNBA today is barely comparable to seven years ago, in a very good way. But with a bigger ecosystem -- to use one of Engelbert's favorite terms -- comes more opportunities and challenges. Other women's sports are growing, too, and while there is camaraderie there, the WNBA also wants to be the premiere women's sports league in the world. That means grassroots involvement and investment globally in girls' basketball. It means figuring out the WNBA's long-term relationship with Unrivaled. It means being a lot smarter about how to use social media for growth and healthy messaging. The WNBA found some new gears in Engelbert's tenure. Now it's time to really step on the gas.

Copeland: A more congenial relationship with the players is always nice in theory, but the general public often forgets that commissioners work for and represent the owners. There will always be conflict. As Kendra noted above, the league often gets itself in trouble for being slow to react when issues arise as opposed to getting out in front of things. Engelbert had a business background and that was her strong suit, but the league was often reactionary to issues that could be predicted. From problems with officiating to the sale of the Connecticut Sun to player safety and the current transgender conversation, the league was often playing catch-up, which further alienated players.

Is the WNBA better off now than it was when Engelbert took over?

Andrews: Without a doubt, yes. The 2026 WNBA has grown and changed exponentially from the version of the league Engelbert inherited in 2019. Purely from a size standpoint, the WNBA has grown from 12 staff members to nearly 100. The new media rights deal increased the league's economic growth, and the footprint has expanded from 12 teams to 15 (and 18 teams by 2030). Two major CBA deals were negotiated and agreed upon by Engelbert, ensuring the players more pay and benefits (which go to retired players as well), and helping land the first million-dollar contracts in league history. The health and sustainability of the WNBA is in a far better place than it was six years ago, and should be set up for far more success under the next commissioner.

Copeland: The league is in a completely different place today than it was in 2018. Now, Engelbert shouldn't get credit for all the advances, but she certainly played a significant role. Kendra hit all the touchpoints, but one thing that has advanced is the talent level in and entering the league. As the WNBA has grown into a sustainable major professional league in the United States in which players can stay at home and make generational wealth, young girls can have this as a goal in a more advanced way than ever before. The trickle down has been more youth programs and training opportunities for girls than in preceding years. Young girls are taking advantage, growing skills and defining goals earlier. It's not a surprise that there has been an influx of talent coming out of the drafts that are making an immediate and historical impact on the league -- Clark, Paige Bueckers, Reese, Olivia Miles, Sonia Citron and Kiki Iriafen to name a few. The depth and talent level in recent drafts has been more consistent and dependable in recent years. That's not directly related to the commissioner's role, but the growth and advanced state of the WNBA has had a direct impact on the youth ranks, which pays off for the league years later.

stories.headline: Winners and losers of Cale Makar's $163.2 million contract
stories.summary: The deal for Colorado's franchise defenseman set a new high benchmark for NHL players, with impacts around the league.
stories.body:
Cale Makar made NHL history last week, becoming the first player to earn $20 million annually in his blockbuster contract extension with the Colorado Avalanche.

His deal is worth $163.2 million over eight seasons. The 27-year-old defenseman's average annual value is $20.8 million against the salary cap. While many anticipated Makar would reset standards with his new contract, the fallout from his deal with Colorado will impact the rest of the NHL.

Some teams, players and trends will end up winners because of it. Others ... not so much.

Here are some winners and losers of the Makar contract.

Winner: Colorado Avalanche
Obviously.

GM Joe Sakic said recently that "you can't win without superstars." That's what you'd expect to hear from a guy who won Stanley Cups as a player on teams that featured Hall of Famers such as Peter Forsberg, Ray Bourque, Rob Blake and this guy Patrick Roy in goal; but also from the guy who built a roster around Makar and center Nathan MacKinnon that produced a Stanley Cup win in 2022.

There's an argument to be made that the Avalanche have the best players in the world at center and on defense and now have them both locked up through 2031. Every team in the league is trying to build a winner. No one has that kind of foundation on which to build.

Sakic was blessed with a star defenseman who wanted to go max term (eight years) from the start of negotiations. No "wait and see" contract. No trying to sync up the end of his deal with that of a family member on another NHL team (more on that in a moment). Cale Makar wanted to give Colorado nine whacks at the piñata while he's under contract.

We can tsk-tsk the Avalanche for not leveraging that commitment into a friendlier cap hit, but the reality is that both Makar and his camp fully understood the current market and the one that Makar could create as an unrestricted free agent next summer. There was no steep discount to be had here, nor should there have been the expectation of one.

There are legit concerns about aging curves and overall health for a player who logs the kind of ice time that Makar does. Teams go into contract talks all the time with that in the back of their throats. But the inherent greatness of Makar, and this window to win with him on the blue line, outweigh those worries.

His cap hit will be recontextualized, as they all eventually are. The NHL is going to have the revenue streams from new media rights deals and at least two new teams inflating the cap during Makar's contract term. As one player agent told me: "By the time this deal is over, there will be guys in the league making $30 million per season."

Loser: Bill Guerin
First off, much respect to the Minnesota GM for facing a barrage of questions during a recent local media tour -- at the Minnesota State Fair, no less! -- about the status of his contract negotiations with Quinn Hughes. We've come to expect that kind of candor from Guerin, as both an NHL executive and U.S. national team general manager, but it's still refreshing when so many of his colleagues get camera shy during high-stakes negotiations.

Guerin told WCCO's Chad Hartman that there's "no tension" with Hughes and his agent, Pat Brisson, but refused to traffic in hypotheticals. Dan Barreiro of KFAN told Guerin he "can't trade" Hughes due to how much the Wild gave the Vancouver Canucks for the defenseman; Guerin reiterated that "we don't want to lose him and our fans don't want to lose him."

Hughes has one more season left at $7.85 million before becoming an unrestricted free agent next summer, and he's eligible to sign an extension now. If he signs before Sept. 15, he can max out at an eight-year term. If he signs as a free agent next summer, the max is six years -- although the max contract he could sign (20% of a projected $113.5 million cap in 2027-28) would be higher, at $22.7 million.

It's hard to find many around the NHL who believe Hughes will sign a long-term deal with the Wild. Most expect it'll be a three-year term that walks him up to 2030 when his brother Jack Hughes of the New Jersey Devils is an unrestricted free agent. But what about the money?

As Guerin did radio hits about Hughes amid the butter sculptures and lumberjack shows at the fair, there was one common theme: That Makar's deal impacts what Hughes could make on a new contract, but not dramatically.

"Could it affect you financially? Yeah. There's the bar with Cale Makar signing that contract in Colorado, but Quinn might be after different things. He's got different things in the life that's important to him," he told Hartman.

Guerin's theory: That Hughes has already made significant money in his career, so he can afford to make different types of decisions on his next contract. His current contract, signed in 2021, is worth $47.1 million.

"It doesn't have to be that 'Makar signed for this so he's got to sign for that.' No. He can do whatever the hell he wants because he's not going broke tomorrow," Guerin told KFAN.

Of course, Makar will have made $54 million on his current deal before starting on a $163 million contract in 2027-28.

It's possible that Guerin would have to overcompensate Hughes regardless of what Makar makes, like he did to keep Kirill Kaprizov in Minnesota. Makar's deal doesn't dramatically change the math on Hughes. It also doesn't uncomplicate what's already an extremely complicated negotiation for Guerin.

Winner: Matthew Schaefer
After just one season with the New York Islanders -- in which he was the unanimous choice for NHL rookie of the year -- Schaefer might already be in blank check territory for his next contract. The defenseman, who turns 19 this week, has that rare franchise-altering alchemy of on-ice ability and off-ice charisma that's been previously exhibited by players like Alex Ovechkin. He's that special.

And soon he'll be very, very rich.

Schaefer can sign an extension next summer as he enters the last year of his rookie contract. Islanders GM Mathieu Darche now has two contractual magnets pulling up Schaefer's salary: Makar, resetting the bar for defensemen at $20.4 million AAV; and San Jose Sharks phenom Macklin Celebrini, another transformative young player who will earn $18.8 million annually over five seasons.

Loser: Columbus Blue Jackets
The current holy trinity of NHL defensemen is Makar, Hughes and Zach Werenski, the latter of whom won the Norris Trophy last season ... and then blocked a trade to the Dallas Stars after communicating that he didn't plan on signing an extension with the Blue Jackets.

Werenski, 29, has since emphasized that he wants to remain in Columbus as long as the Blue Jackets are a playoff team that's trending in the right direction.

He's eligible to sign an extension next summer, with two years remaining on a deal that carries a $9,583,334 average annual value. The ceiling for Werenski as a 2028 free agent would be an AAV of $24.6 million. Whether or not his heart's still in Columbus could be a separate issue from whether the Blue Jackets would commit that kind of money for any player -- let alone a defenseman who will be in his early 30s by then.

Winner: Montreal Canadiens
Lane Hutson finished one point behind Cale Makar in scoring among defensemen last season. In 2027-28, when he's 23 years old, Hutson will count $11.55 million less against the salary cap than Makar does.

There are mitigating circumstances for Montreal's deal with Hutson, which he signed last October in the final season of his rookie contract. The defenseman was a 10.2(c) restricted free agent, leaving him with little leverage as a player ineligible for either an offer sheet or arbitration. But Montreal used that advantage to squeeze an eight-year deal with an $8.85 million annual cap hit out of Hutson.

It was praised as a bargain at the time -- many felt he'd at least hit $10 million AAV -- but given how the ground shifted after Makar's deal for scoring defensemen, it's an absolute steal.

This is going to be for Montreal like MacKinnon's second contract was for Colorado (seven years at $6.3 million annually): an epic underpayment of an elite player that allows his team to get a ton of other business done. Keep in mind the Avalanche won the Stanley Cup in Year 6 of that deal.

Loser: Analytics truthers
Cale Makar has been a Norris Trophy finalist in six of his seven NHL seasons, winning it twice and finishing second in the voting twice as well. He has a Calder Trophy and a Conn Smythe to his credit. He's considered the best defenseman of his generation, perhaps even the best player of his generation. Comparisons to Bobby Orr aren't met with a scoff but with respectful contemplation.

But there's another assessment of Makar -- in the present and for the duration of his contract -- that's worth considering: The one from analytics-driven skeptics who see Makar's deified status as more than a little bit owed to the greatness of MacKinnon.

Corey Sznajder had a nuanced look at this theory on All Three Zones, which included these numbers from Natural Stat Trick:

"Over the past three seasons, Makar has shared the ice with MacKinnon for 2,572 minutes compared to 1,434 minutes without him (all 5v5 by the way). In those minutes, the Avs own 58.1% of the shot attempts, 57.4% of the expected goals and 61.3% of the goals. In the minutes with Makar without MacKinnon the ice, Colorado owns only 47.3% of the shots, 48% of the expected goals and 52.2% of the goals. MacKinnon without Makar on the ice is at 56.6%, 55.7% and 66.8% in all three of those stats respectively," Sznajder wrote.

Those kinds of stats don't necessarily paint their on-ice partnership as symbiotic, but rather MacKinnon being the one driving the bus, while Makar stands over his shoulder like Keanu with Sandra Bullock in "Speed."

Obviously, the Avalanche don't care about any of this after giving Makar a record-breaking contract. He and MacKinnon are going to share the ice for Colorado until 2031 at a minimum. But this conjecture will continue to simmer in awards debates, player comparisons on social media and now in evaluating Makar under this megadeal.

Winner: player empowerment
As I wrote in June, the age of player empowerment is at hand for the NHL. We saw it in Brady Tkachuk leveraging a trade to his brother's team in South Florida, or in Dylan Larkin trying to force his way out of a long-term commitment to the Detroit Red Wings. But we also saw it in some of the mega-contracts that we signed in the offseason, with Makar's deal as the current apex.

Young stars like Celebrini ($18.8 million AAV) and Chicago's Connor Bedard ($15 million AAV) scored big in re-signing with their teams. Leo Carlsson shocked the NHL by signing a five-year, $18 million AAV offer sheet with the Philadelphia Flyers that the Anaheim Ducks matched.

(My favorite theory of the offseason, offered up by one NHL player agent: That Flyers ownership greenlit the Carlsson offer sheet as the ultimate long-term vengeance in the Cutter Gauthier drama with Anaheim. "They probably want to say, 'Hey, Philly's a good spot to be in. Don't [mess] with us.'")

There are always going to be players who take a "team-friendly" deal because the circumstances warrant it, like Connor McDavid earning less annually than Leon Draisaitl. But the ones breaking the bank are no longer the outliers, and they're going to keep breaking it. Some NHL teams are projecting the salary cap could rise to $150-$160 million by the 2031-32 season. Makar is just the beginning.

(Although, technically, Makar did just sign a team-friendly deal: $400,000 annually under the max, and one year before unrestricted free agency could have upped his ask to over $22 million annually.)

Loser: Short-term deals
Perhaps the most shocking aspect of Makar's extension wasn't the money but the term.

One hallmark of the NHL's player empowerment trend has been contract duration. Auston Matthews was one of the first huge names to go short-term, signing a five-year deal with the Toronto Maple Leafs in 2019 and then a four-year extension in 2023. Since then, Celebrini, Bedard, Carlsson and Nico Hischier of the New Jersey Devils have all signed five-year extensions, while defenseman Evan Bouchard went four years with the Edmonton Oilers.

But Makar's focus from the start of talks with the Avalanche was an eight-year term, an option that will not exist when the new CBA kicks in later this month.

"I think it gives us a lot of clarity in the sense of the direction we want to go in, hopefully being able to succeed in the next nine years, and have that stability in knowing that the contract is there and we have the pieces that we can build around," he said, via NHL.com.

Again, not everyone in the NHL can look around their locker room and see Nathan MacKinnon, with the proof of concept of having already won a Stanley Cup with him. Makar didn't have to take the "wait and see" deal that others in his tax bracket have with teams striving to become contenders. Makar knows what he has around him. And now, the Avalanche know they have Makar for the next decade.

stories.headline: 'I'll definitely be back': Sloan vows NRL return as Cook closes 13-year loop
stories.summary: Tyrell Sloan and Damien Cook will head to Castleford together in 2027, but the departing Dragons left the NRL at opposite stages of their careers after a fairytale finish in Wollongong.
stories.body:
Tyrell Sloan has vowed his spectacular St George Illawarra farewell will not be his final act in the NRL, declaring he will "definitely be back" following a match-winning performance against Parramatta.

Sloan will head to Castleford alongside Damien Cook in 2027, the departing Dragons leaving the NRL at contrasting stages of their careers but on a collective high after a fairytale finish in Wollongong.

Playing his 97th and final game for his junior club, Sloan scored a first-half try before drilling a 43-metre two-point field goal in the 74th minute to seal a dramatic 24-22 comeback victory at a sold-out WIN Stadium.

It was the first field goal of Sloan's NRL career and ensured the 24-year-old departed the Dragons with one of the most memorable moments of his six seasons in the Red V.

"I don't reckon it'll be the last time you see me in the NRL. I'll definitely be back," Sloan told ESPN.

"Regardless of what jersey I put on, I'll always have the Red V at heart."

Sloan is preparing to join Castleford on a two-year deal from next season, alongside Dragons teammates Damien Cook and Mathew Feagai.

While the long-range strike appeared improbable to most inside the stadium, Sloan revealed it was a skill he had repeatedly attempted between training drills - often to the frustration of coach Dean Young.

"It was just off the cuff, some things we do throughout the week. I was actually practicing this for fun," Sloan said.

"Youngy usually gets pissed off because in between drills I'm just trying to slot them from 40 out and kicking all his balls away that he's using for the next drill.

"We had a little laugh there. He goes, 'Maybe I'll let you do a little bit more.'

"I wasn't sure if it was going over looking from our end, but luckily it did. The boys got around me, which was a really good feeling."

The victory could not prevent the Dragons from collecting the first wooden spoon in the joint venture's history, but it provided a fitting send-off for a host of departing players and snapped the club's 400-day wait for a victory in Wollongong.

For Sloan, a Dapto junior who progressed through the Dragons' pathways before making a try-scoring NRL debut in 2021, the reality of leaving his only NRL club had not yet sunk in.

"I guess it hasn't really sunk in, the possibility of leaving," he said.

"If I'm not here, I'll be watching the Red V from afar and cheering them on because, at the end of the day, it's always going to be a big part of my career and they'll always have my heart, for sure."

While Sloan expects another NRL chapter, Cook's journey in the competition has reached its conclusion.

The 35-year-old finished with 263 NRL appearances after beginning his career with the Dragons in 2013, spending two seasons with Canterbury and nine with South Sydney before returning home to captain St George Illawarra across the past two years.

Cook initially believed he had kept his emotions under control after full-time, before spotting former Rabbitohs teammates Jai Arrow, Cody Walker and Cameron Murray in the crowd and then reuniting with his family.

"I thought I was going all right, and then I saw a couple of the teammates, the Souths boys, and got a bit emotional," Cook told ESPN.

"It really got me when I saw my family, especially my wife.

"It was pretty special to have those guys turn up. I spent a long time there and a lot of time with them.

"That's one of the great things about the game - it gives you those mates and those memories."

Cook admitted the finality of his NRL retirement may not fully register until his former teammates return for preseason training without him.

"I think it probably will more when preseason starts and I'm not going back to preseason," he said.

"I'll sit back at home while they're getting flogged in the heat and I've got to worry about training in minus-five degrees. That'll be different.

"But I know in my heart it's the right time. I made the decision early for my family and myself, and I've never looked back.

"It has given me a good chance to really enjoy the rest of the season."

Asked what advice he would give the version of himself who debuted for the Dragons 13 years ago, Cook provided a fitting summation of his career.

"Keep working hard to get it, because it's going to be a hell of a ride," he said.

"It's going to be good fun, so enjoy it. Try and soak it up as much as possible."
